mainTopic: The coming of משיח: the suffering before him, his name and identity, and the day of ה׳
overview: This amud is all about the coming of משיח. It opens with the end of a description of foreign armies overrunning the land. Then רב says משיח will come only after the evil kingdom rules over ישראל for nine months. עולא, רבה and later רבי יוחנן say they would rather not live to see משיח, because of the terrible suffering before he comes. רב יוסף disagrees and would accept any disgrace just to be there. רבה explains that even תורה and חסד may not protect him, since sin can cancel protection, as with יעקב's fear and the second entry into the land. רבי יוחנן explains his fear from a פסוק in ירמיה about the pain of that time. The גמרא then discusses whether ישראל will enjoy the years of משיח, for whom the world was created, what משיח's name is, who he might be, and how a 'new דוד' will rule beside the original דוד. It ends with רבי שמלאי's parable of the rooster and the bat about the day of ה׳.

steps.title: Why the coffin must be buried deep
steps.stepSummary: This is the end of a statement that began before this section. The speaker explains that in the coming wars, foreign horses will be tied to every palm tree in בבל, and Median horses will eat straw out of every coffin in ארץ ישראל.
steps.simpleTranslation: For there is no palm tree in בבל that a Persian horse will not be tied to, and there is no coffin in ארץ ישראל that a Median horse will not eat straw from.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a statement that started earlier. It describes how complete the foreign takeover will be before משיח comes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The speaker is giving the reason for his request, which appears before this section. The armies will be everywhere: every palm tree will be used as a hitching post. Even coffins will be dug up and used as feeding troughs for the horses.

keyTerms.meaning: Median, from the land of Media

phrases.english: for there is no palm tree in Babylonia

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין סוּס שֶׁל פָּרְסִיִּים נִקְשָׁר בּוֹ,
phrases.english: to which a horse of the Persians will not be tied,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין לָךְ כׇּל אָרוֹן וְאָרוֹן שֶׁבְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל,
phrases.english: and there is no coffin in Eretz Yisrael

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁאֵין סוּס מָדִי אוֹכֵל בּוֹ תֶּבֶן.
phrases.english: from which a Median horse will not eat straw.
phrases.notes: He means the coffins will be dug up and used as feeding troughs for the horses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a statement that began before this section
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Before the גאולה, foreign armies will overrun both בבל and ארץ ישראל completely, and even graves will not be left alone.

steps.title: Nine months of the evil kingdom before משיח
steps.stepSummary: רב teaches that בן דוד will not come until the evil kingdom spreads over ישראל for nine months. He learns this from a פסוק in מיכה that compares the wait to a pregnancy.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב says: בן דוד will not come until the evil kingdom spreads over ישראל for nine months, as it says: 'Therefore He will give them up until the time that she who is giving birth has given birth; then the rest of his brothers will return with בני ישראל.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב gives a new sign for when משיח will come, and he brings a פסוק as his source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק speaks about the time 'until she who is giving birth has given birth.' A pregnancy lasts nine months, so רב reads the פסוק as saying the hard period of foreign rule will last nine months. After that, the 'birth', meaning the גאולה, comes.

keyTerms.meaning: The son of David, meaning משיח

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב: אֵין בֶּן דָּוִד בָּא
phrases.english: Rav says: The son of David will not come
until the evil kingdom spreads out
over Israel for nine months,
as it is stated: “Therefore He will give them up
phrases.notes: מיכה 5:2

phrases.english: until the time when she who is giving birth has given birth;
phrases.notes: A pregnancy lasts nine months. That is where רב gets his number.

phrases.aramaic: וְיֶתֶר אֶחָיו יְשׁוּבוּן עַל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל״.
phrases.english: then the rest of his brothers will return with the children of Israel.”

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: אֵין בֶּן דָּוִד בָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another sign of the time before משיח, alongside the description of foreign takeover in step 1
steps.mimraCoreRuling: משיח comes after the evil kingdom rules over ישראל for nine months, learned from the 'birth' image in מיכה 5:2.

steps.title: עולא and רבה would rather not see משיח come
steps.stepSummary: עולא says, 'Let משיח come, but let me not see him.' רבה says the same thing.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא says: Let him come, but I do not want to see him. And רבה also says: Let him come, but I do not want to see him.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים say they want משיח to come, but they hope it happens after they are no longer alive.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They are not against משיח coming. They are afraid of the terrible suffering that comes right before it, which the earlier steps described. So they wish to be spared from living through that period.

keyTerms.meaning: But let me not see him

steps.confusionAlert: עולא and רבה are not saying they don't want משיח! They want him to come. They are only afraid of living through the suffering before he arrives.

phrases.english: Ulla says:
Let him come, but let me not see him.
phrases.notes: He means: let משיח come after I am gone.

phrases.english: And likewise Rabba says:
phrases.notes: The square brackets mean the corrected wording reads רבה here. That fits, since אביי later questions רבה.

phrases.english: Let him come, but let me not see him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reacts to the descriptions of hard times before משיח
steps.mimraCoreRuling: עולא and רבה hope משיח comes only after their lifetime, so they do not have to live through the suffering before him.

steps.title: רב יוסף wants to see משיח no matter the cost
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף disagrees. He says, 'Let משיח come, and may I merit to sit even in the shade of his donkey's dung.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף says: Let him come, and may I merit to sit in the shade of the dung of his donkey.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף gives the opposite view: he wants to be there when משיח comes, even if it is painful and humbling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Sitting 'in the shade of his donkey's dung' is a picture of the lowest, most humbling place. רב יוסף is saying he will accept any suffering or disgrace, as long as he gets to see משיח.

phrases.english: Rav Yosef says:
Let him come, and may I merit
to sit in the shade
of the dung of his donkey.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב יוֹסֵף אָמַר: יֵיתֵי וְאֶזְכֵּי דְּאֵיתֵיב בְּטוּלָּא דְּכוּפִיתָא דַּחֲמָרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with עולא and רבה in step 3
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב יוסף is willing to suffer any pain or disgrace in order to see משיח.

steps.title: אביי asks רבה why he is afraid
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks רבה for the reason behind his fear. He suggests that maybe it is because of חבלו של משיח, the pains before משיח comes.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to רבה: What is the reason? If we say it is because of the birth pains of משיח...
steps.whatsHappening: אביי questions רבה's statement from step 3. He suggests a possible reason, and this sets up his challenge in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'אילימא' ('if we say') offers the obvious reason for רבה's fear: the suffering before משיח. אביי is not accepting this reason. He brings it up so he can knock it down in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: If we say; introduces a suggested answer that will be challenged
The birth pains of משיח, meaning the suffering before he comes

phrases.english: Abaye said to Rabba:
What is the reason?
phrases.notes: He is asking why רבה said, back in step 3, that he did not want to see משיח.

phrases.english: If we say it is because of the birth pains of the Messiah?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי לְרַבָּה: מַאי טַעְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions רבה's statement from step 3
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רבה does not want to live to see משיח, and whether it is because of חבלו של משיח.

steps.title: תורה and חסד protect from the pains, and רבה has both
steps.stepSummary: אביי brings a ברייתא. רבי אלעזר's students asked how a person can be saved from חבלו של משיח, and he answered: by learning תורה and doing גמילות חסדים. רבה has plenty of both, so why should he be afraid?
steps.simpleTranslation: But it was taught: רבי אלעזר's students asked him, 'What should a person do to be saved from the birth pains of משיח?' He said: 'He should be busy with תורה and acts of kindness.' And you, Master, have both תורה and acts of kindness!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי challenges the suggested reason for רבה's fear. A ברייתא says that תורה and kindness protect a person, and רבה has both.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא offers a cure for חבלו של משיח: תורה and גמילות חסדים. Since רבה is known for both, he should be protected, so the suffering should not be a reason for him to fear. רבה answers this challenge in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Master; a respectful way of saying 'you'

steps.whatToRemember: According to the ברייתא, learning תורה and doing גמילות חסדים protect a person from חבלו של משיח. So אביי asks why רבה, who has both, is still afraid.

phrases.english: But isn't it taught:
His students asked Rabbi Elazar:
What should a person do
to be saved from the birth pains of the Messiah?
He should be busy with Torah and with acts of kindness.
And the Master: here is Torah
phrases.notes: Now אביי is speaking again, pointing to רבה himself.

phrases.english: and here are acts of kindness!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָתַנְיָא: שָׁאֲלוּ תַּלְמִידָיו אֶת רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reason suggested in step 5
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that רבה fears seeing משיח because of חבלו של משיח
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא teaches that תורה and גמילות חסדים save a person from חבלו של משיח. רבה has both, so he should be protected and should have nothing to fear.

steps.title: רבה fears that sin may cancel his protection
steps.stepSummary: רבה answers אביי: he is afraid that sin may cancel the protection that תורה and גמילות חסדים give. He supports this with רבי יעקב בר אידי.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said to him: Maybe sin will cause it, like the teaching of רבי יעקב בר אידי.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה answers אביי's challenge from step 6. He says that even with all his good deeds, he is afraid that sin could cancel his protection.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי assumed that תורה and חסד automatically protect a person. רבה agrees they protect, but says a sin could undo that protection. He is about to bring support from רבי יעקב בר אידי.

keyTerms.meaning: Maybe sin will cause it, meaning a sin may cancel a promise or protection

phrases.english: He said to him: Perhaps sin will cause it,
phrases.notes: רבה is answering אביי. He means a sin might cancel the protection he would otherwise have.

phrases.english: like the teaching of Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's challenge in step 6.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Adds a hidden factor: protection can be cancelled by sin.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: תורה and חסד guarantee protection, so רבה should not be afraid.
steps.terutzMaskana: The protection is real, but a sin could cancel it, so fear still makes sense.

steps.title: רבי יעקב בר אידי's contradiction about יעקב's fear
steps.stepSummary: רבי יעקב בר אידי points out two פסוקים that seem to clash. ה׳ promised to guard יעקב, yet יעקב was very afraid of עשו.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יעקב בר אידי pointed out a contradiction. It says: 'I am with you and I will guard you wherever you go.' And it also says: 'יעקב was very afraid and distressed.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the teaching of רבי יעקב בר אידי that רבה relies on. It begins with a question: why was יעקב afraid if ה׳ promised to protect him?
steps.deeperAnalysis: ה׳'s promise in בראשית 28 should have taken away any fear. So יעקב's fear in בראשית 32 needs an explanation. The answer in the next step will be the source for רבה's fear.

keyTerms.meaning: He raised a contradiction between two sources
It is written... and it is written (two פסוקים set against each other)

phrases.english: For Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi raised a contradiction:
It is written: "And behold, I am with you,
and I will guard you wherever you go,"
phrases.notes: בראשית 28:15

phrases.english: and it is written: "And Yaakov was very afraid and distressed."
phrases.notes: בראשית 32:8, when יעקב heard עשו was coming toward him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Quotes the source that רבה mentioned in step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: How the two פסוקים about יעקב fit together.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If ה׳ promised protection, יעקב should not have been afraid.

steps.title: יעקב feared his sin might cancel the promise
steps.stepSummary: The answer: יעקב was afraid that some sin of his might cancel ה׳'s promise.
steps.simpleTranslation: He was afraid that maybe sin would cause the promise to be cancelled.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יעקב בר אידי answers his own question. יעקב trusted the promise, but he worried that a sin might cancel it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This settles the contradiction: the promise was real, but it depended on staying worthy. This is exactly רבה's worry: his merits protect him only as long as sin does not cancel them.
steps.whatToRemember: A promise from ה׳ can be lost through sin, so even a great צדיק like יעקב was afraid.

phrases.english: For he was afraid that perhaps sin would cause it,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 8.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains that the promise had a condition.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A promise from ה׳ means there is nothing to fear.
steps.terutzMaskana: A promise can be cancelled by sin, so fear is still right.

steps.title: A ברייתא about the two entries into the land
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא reads the two halves of a פסוק in אז ישיר as talking about two entries into ארץ ישראל: the first one and the second one.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught: 'Until Your people pass over, ה׳' is the first entry. 'Until this people You acquired pass over' is the second entry.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to prove that sin can cancel what was promised. This step lays out the ברייתא; the next step draws the lesson from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק repeats 'until they pass over' twice. The ברייתא says this hints at two entries into the land. Putting both in the same פסוק suggests both should have come with the same open miracles.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught in a ברייתא
The first entry into ארץ ישראל
The second entry into ארץ ישראל

phrases.english: As it was taught in a ברייתא:
"Until Your people pass over, ה׳"
phrases.notes: שמות 15:16

phrases.english: this is the first entry,
phrases.notes: The first entry is coming into the land with יהושע. The second is returning from בבל in the time of עזרא.

phrases.english: "until this people You acquired pass over"
this is the second entry.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings proof for the idea in step 9 that sin can cancel a promise.
steps.raayaObject: That sin can cancel something good that ה׳ would otherwise do.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא reading שמות 15:16 as talking about two entries into the land.

steps.title: The second entry lacked miracles because of sin
steps.stepSummary: The lesson of the ברייתא: Israel deserved open miracles in the second entry, like the first, but sin stopped it.
steps.simpleTranslation: So say from now: Israel deserved to have a miracle done for them in the second entry, like in the first entry, but sin caused it not to happen.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the conclusion from the ברייתא. This finishes the proof that sin can cancel a good outcome.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since both entries are in one פסוק, both should have had the same miracles. But the return from בבל was quiet, and the Jews stayed under foreign rule, because of sin. This backs up יעקב's fear, and so also רבה's fear.

keyTerms.meaning: Say from now, meaning 'so we can conclude'

steps.whatToRemember: רבה's answer is complete: good deeds protect, but sin can cancel the protection. יעקב and the return from בבל both show this, so even a great person can fear the pains before משיח.

phrases.english: Say from now:

phrases.aramaic: רְאוּיִים הָיוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל לַעֲשׂוֹת לָהֶם נֵס
phrases.english: Israel were worthy to have a miracle done for them
in the second entry like in the first entry,
but the sin caused it not to happen.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the lesson from the ברייתא in step 10.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Sin can cancel what Israel deserved, so fearing that sin may cancel protection is justified.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן also does not want to see משיח
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says the same as עולא and רבה: let משיח come, but let me not see him.
steps.simpleTranslation: And so said רבי יוחנן: Let him come, but let me not see him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another great אמורא, רבי יוחנן, who shares the same wish as עולא and רבה. This sets up a new discussion about his reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן says the same words as step 3. The word וכן ('and so') shows he agrees with them. Next ריש לקיש will ask what his reason is.

keyTerms.meaning: Let him come, but let me not see him

phrases.english: And so said Rabbi Yochanan:
Let him come, but let me not see him.
phrases.notes: "Him" means משיח, like the same words back in step 3.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: יֵיתֵי וְלָא אִיחְמִינֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another opinion matching עולא and רבה in step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יוחנן also hopes משיח comes, but not in his lifetime.

steps.title: ריש לקיש asks for the reason and suggests one
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש asks רבי יוחנן why he is afraid. He suggests it may be because of a פסוק in עמוס about running from one danger right into another.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said to him: What is the reason? If you say it is because it is written: 'As when a man runs from a lion and a bear meets him, and he comes home and leans his hand on the wall and a snake bites him'?
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש asks for רבי יוחנן's reason and offers a possible one. This sets up the next step, where he will push back on that reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in עמוס describes the day of ה׳ as one disaster after another with no escape. That could explain the fear of the time of משיח. The word אילימא ('if you say') warns us that ריש לקיש is about to reject this suggestion.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (usually a suggestion that will be rejected)

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ: מַאי טַעְמָא?
phrases.english: Reish Lakish said to him: What is the reason?
If you say it is because it is written:
"As when a man flees from the lion,
and the bear meets him, [and he came into the house]
phrases.notes: The words in square brackets are added to match the פסוק.

phrases.aramaic: וְסָמַךְ יָדוֹ עַל הַקִּיר וּנְשָׁכוֹ הַנָּחָשׁ״?
phrases.english: and he leaned his hand on the wall and the snake bit him"?
phrases.notes: עמוס 5:19

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ: מַאי טַעְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reason behind רבי יוחנן's statement in step 12.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why רבי יוחנן does not want to see משיח.

steps.title: These troubles already happen in this world
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש pushes back: the troubles in the פסוק already happen today. A guard in the field is like a lion, a tax collector in the city is like a bear, and hungry children at home are like a snake bite.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and I will show you an example of this in this world: When a person goes out to the field and a guard confronts him, it is like being met by a lion. He enters the city and a tax collector confronts him; it is like being met by a bear. He enters his house and finds his sons and daughters lying hungry; it is like being bitten by a snake.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש shows that every trouble in the פסוק already exists in normal life today. So this פסוק is not a good reason to fear the time of משיח.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If these sufferings are already part of this world, they are nothing special about the days before משיח. That removes the suggested reason for רבי יוחנן's fear. The גמרא will still need to find a different reason.

keyTerms.meaning: Its example, something just like it
A field guard or official who demands payment

steps.confusionAlert: ריש לקיש is not saying the פסוק is false. He is saying its troubles are already here now, so they cannot explain why someone would fear the days of משיח in particular.

phrases.english: Come and I will show you its example in this world:
When a person goes out to the field
and a guard confronts him,
it is like one whom a lion met.
He enters the city, and a tax collector confronts him;
it is like one whom a bear met.
He enters his house
and finds his sons and daughters lying in hunger;
it is like one whom a snake bit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the reason suggested in step 13.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only the suggested reason (the פסוק in עמוס), not רבי יוחנן's statement itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The troubles in the פסוק already happen in this world, so they are not special to the time of משיח.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן gives his real reason: a פסוק in ירמיה
steps.stepSummary: After ריש לקיש rejected his suggested reason, רבי יוחנן explains that his fear comes from a פסוק in ירמיה describing terrible pain, like childbirth, in the days of משיח.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it is because it is written: "Ask now and see whether a male gives birth. Why do I see every man with his hands on his loins like a woman in labor, and all faces turned green?"
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן now gives his true reason for not wanting to see משיח. It is a פסוק in ירמיה that describes awful pain at that time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: ריש לקיש had shown that the troubles in the עמוס פסוק already happen every day, so they cannot be the reason. רבי יוחנן agrees and points to a different פסוק, which describes something worse: even grown men twisting in pain like a woman giving birth. The next steps will explain who that 'man' really is.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, instead (drops the earlier idea and gives a new one)
Because it is written (introduces a פסוק as the reason)
A green or pale color, how a face looks from fear

phrases.english: Rather, it is because it is written:
phrases.notes: רבי יוחנן is speaking. He drops the reason ריש לקיש suggested and gives his own.

phrases.english: "Ask now and see
phrases.notes: ירמיה 30:6

phrases.english: whether a male gives birth;
why do I see every man
with his hands on his loins like a woman giving birth,
and all faces turned green?"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the reason that ריש לקיש rejected in step 14 with the real reason.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why is רבי יוחנן afraid to see משיח?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Because of the פסוק in ירמיה describing childbirth-like pain at that time.

steps.title: Who is the 'man' in the פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what 'every man' means, and רבא בר יצחק in the name of רב answers that it refers to הקב״ה, the One Who has all strength.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is "I see every man"? רבא בר יצחק said in the name of רב: It means the One to Whom all strength belongs.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the words 'every man' in the פסוק. רב says it refers to הקב״ה Himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word גבר sounds like גבורה, strength, so כל גבר is read as 'the One with all strength.' This means that, so to speak, even הקב״ה is pained at that time. That is a much deeper reason for fear than ordinary human troubles.

keyTerms.meaning: A man, connected here to גְּבוּרָה
What is (asks for the meaning of words)

steps.confusionAlert: The 'man' with hands on his loins here is not a regular person. רב reads it as הקב״ה, described in human terms.

phrases.english: What is "I see every man"?

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רָבָא בַּר יִצְחָק אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rava bar Yitzchak said in the name of Rav:
The One to Whom all strength belongs.
phrases.notes: He reads גבר as coming from גבורה, strength, so it means הקב״ה Himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains a phrase from the פסוק quoted in step 15.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does 'every man' in the פסוק mean?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It refers to הקב״ה, the One with all strength.

steps.title: Why all faces turn pale
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that the angels above and ישראל below turn pale when הקב״ה says that both ישראל and the nations are His handiwork, and asks how He can destroy one for the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is "and all faces turned green"? רבי יוחנן said: The household above and the household below, at the time when הקב״ה says: These are My handiwork and those are My handiwork, how can I destroy these because of those?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the end of the פסוק, about faces turning green. רבי יוחנן says everyone above and below becomes frightened when הקב״ה hesitates to destroy the nations for ישראל's sake.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saving ישראל means punishing the nations. But הקב״ה says both are His creations and asks how He can destroy one because of the other. That hesitation scares the angels and ישראל, and this is why רבי יוחנן feared that time.

keyTerms.meaning: The heavenly household, meaning the angels
The work of My hands, My creations

steps.whyThisMatters: This completes רבי יוחנן's reason: the danger is not ordinary trouble but that, at that moment, ישראל might not be clearly favored over the nations.

phrases.english: And what is "and all faces turned green"?
Rabbi Yochanan said:
The household above
and the household below,
at the time when the Holy One, Blessed be He, says:
These are My handiwork
and those are My handiwork,
phrases.notes: One 'these' is ישראל and the other is the nations.

phrases.english: how can I destroy these because of those?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the second half of the same פסוק from step 15.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What does 'all faces turned green' mean?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Angels and ישראל grow pale when הקב״ה hesitates to destroy the nations, who are also His handiwork.

steps.title: רב פפא's proverb about the ox and the horse
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא compares this to a farmer whose ox falls, so he puts a horse in its place.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: This is what people say: The ox runs and falls, and the owner goes and puts the horse in its stall.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא adds a common saying that fits the idea from step 17.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ox is the better work animal, but when it falls, the owner makes do with a horse. In the same way, when ישראל fall through sin, it is as if their special place is handed over to the nations. That is why ישראל's position at that time is frightening.

keyTerms.meaning: This is what people say (introduces a common saying)

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן's fear of seeing משיח comes from the ירמיה פסוק: even הקב״ה is pained, and He hesitates to destroy the nations for ישראל, like a horse replacing a fallen ox.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:
This is what people say:
The ox runs and falls,
and he goes and puts
the horse in its stall.
phrases.notes: The owner puts the horse at the ox's feeding place. The ox is ישראל, and the horse is the nations.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Illustrates step 17 with a folk saying.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When ישראל fall, their role is, so to speak, given to the nations, like a horse replacing a fallen ox.

steps.title: ישראל will enjoy the years of משיח
steps.stepSummary: רב גידל in the name of רב says that ישראל are destined to enjoy the good years of משיח.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב גידל said in the name of רב: ישראל are destined to eat the years of משיח.
steps.whatsHappening: A new statement begins. רב teaches that ישראל will enjoy the blessings of the days of משיח.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To 'eat the years' means to enjoy the good that those years bring. This sounds simple, so the next step will ask why רב needed to say it at all.

keyTerms.meaning: Are destined, will in the future

phrases.english: Rav Giddel said in the name of Rav:
Israel are destined
to eat the years of the Messiah.
phrases.notes: 'Eat' here means enjoy the good of those years.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new piece about the days of משיח.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ישראל will enjoy the blessings of the years of משיח.

steps.title: רב יוסף: Isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף asks why רב needed to say this, since obviously ישראל will be the ones to enjoy those years.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: That's obvious! Then who else would eat them? Will Chilak and Bilak eat them?
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף challenges רב's statement as too obvious to need saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The days of משיח are promised to ישראל, so of course ישראל will enjoy them. רב יוסף mocks the idea that anyone else could, naming two made-up nobodies. The challenge is that רב's teaching seems to add nothing new.

keyTerms.meaning: It's obvious! (challenges a statement as adding nothing)

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said: That's obvious!
Then who else would eat them?
Will Chilak and Bilak eat them?
phrases.notes: These are silly made-up names, like saying 'some random nobodies.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the statement in step 19 as obvious.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's statement that ישראל will enjoy the years of משיח
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Who else could possibly enjoy them? The statement seems to teach nothing new.

steps.title: It rejects רבי הילל's view
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that רב's statement comes to reject רבי הילל, who said there is no future משיח because the promises were already fulfilled in the days of חזקיה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It comes to exclude the view of רבי הילל, who said: There is no משיח for ישראל, since they already ate him in the days of חזקיה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers רב יוסף: רב's statement is not obvious, because someone disagreed with it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי הילל held that the משיח promises were already 'eaten', meaning fulfilled, in the time of King חזקיה, so no future משיח will come. רב's teaching that ישראל will still enjoy the years of משיח comes to reject that view.

keyTerms.meaning: There is no משיח for ישראל
חזקיה, the righteous king of יהודה

steps.whatToRemember: רב's teaching that ישראל will enjoy the years of משיח is needed to reject רבי הילל, who held that the משיח promises were already used up in the days of חזקיה.
steps.confusionAlert: 'Ate him' does not mean anything physical. It means the promises about משיח were already used up, fulfilled in חזקיה's time.

phrases.english: It comes to exclude the view of Rabbi Hillel,
who said: There is no Messiah for Israel,
since they already ate him in the days of Hezekiah.
phrases.notes: He means the משיח promises were already fulfilled back then.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב יוסף's challenge from step 20.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifies a disputing opinion that the statement comes to reject
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב's statement seemed obvious, since only ישראל could enjoy the years of משיח.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is needed to reject רבי הילל, who held that משיח already came, in a sense, in חזקיה's days.

steps.title: For whom was the world created?
steps.stepSummary: רב says the world was created only for דוד, שמואל says for משה, and רבי יוחנן says for משיח.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: The world was created only for דוד. שמואל said: For משה. רבי יוחנן said: For משיח.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings three אמוראים who argue about whose merit the world was created for.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each answer points to a different central figure. דוד is the king, משה is the giver of the תורה, and משיח is the final redeemer. רבי יוחנן's answer leads the גמרא into more discussion about משיח.

keyTerms.meaning: For דוד (for his sake and merit)

phrases.english: Rav said:
The world was created only for David.
And Shmuel said: For Moshe.
And Rabbi Yochanan said: For Mashiach.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: לָא אִבְּרִי עָלְמָא אֶלָּא לְדָוִד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new set of statements about משיח, after the discussion of the years of משיח in steps 19-21.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There is a three-way argument about whose merit the world was created for: דוד (רב), משה (שמואל), or משיח (רבי יוחנן).

steps.title: What is the name of משיח?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what משיח's name is.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is his name?
steps.whatsHappening: Since רבי יוחנן just mentioned משיח, the גמרא asks what his name is. This question sets up the list of answers in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a real question asking for information, not a challenge. The answers that follow are mostly about how each group describes משיח through a פסוק.

phrases.english: What is his name?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows up on רבי יוחנן's mention of משיח in step 22.

steps.title: Each school gives משיח a name from a פסוק
steps.stepSummary: The school of רבי שילא says שילה, the school of רבי ינאי says ינון, the school of רבי חנינא says חנינה, some say מנחם בן חזקיה, and the רבנן say 'the leper of the house of רבי'. Each brings a פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: The school of רבי שילא says: His name is שילה, as it says 'Until שילה comes.' The school of רבי ינאי says: His name is ינון, as it says 'May his name last forever, as long as the sun his name will be ינון.' The school of רבי חנינא says: His name is חנינה, as it says 'For I will not give you חנינה (favor).' Some say: His name is מנחם בן חזקיה, as it says 'For the comforter (מנחם) who would revive my soul is far from me.' The רבנן say: His name is 'the pale one of the house of רבי', as it says 'Indeed, he carried our sicknesses and bore our pains, yet we thought him stricken, struck by God, and suffering.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives five answers to the question of משיח's name. Each one is supported by a פסוק that contains that word or describes that idea.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Notice that the first three schools each pick a name that sounds like their own teacher's name: שילה, ינון, and חנינה. מנחם means 'comforter', and the רבנן describe משיח as someone who suffers with illness, based on the פסוק in ישעיהו about carrying our pains.

keyTerms.meaning: The school of / the house of
The pale one, a person with צרעת

steps.confusionAlert: These are not five different people competing to be משיח. Each school is describing משיח with a name taken from a פסוק, and many of the names match the name of that school's own teacher.

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Sheila say:
Shiloh is his name, as it is said:
"Until Shiloh comes."
phrases.notes: בראשית 49:10

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yannai say:
Yinnon is his name, as it is said:
"May his name be forever;
as long as the sun, his name shall continue (yinnon)."
phrases.notes: תהלים 72:17

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Chanina say:
Chanina is his name, as it is said:
"For I will not give you favor (chanina)."
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 16:13

phrases.english: And some say:
Menachem ben Chizkiyah is his name, as it is said:
"For far from me is
the comforter (menachem) who would revive my soul."
phrases.notes: איכה 1:16

phrases.english: And the Rabbis say:
"The pale one of the house of Rebbi" is his name, as it is said:
phrases.notes: Literally 'the white one', meaning someone with צרעת. 'רבי' here is רבי יהודה הנשיא.

phrases.english: "Indeed, he carried our sicknesses,
and he bore our pains,
yet we thought of him as afflicted,
struck by God, and suffering."
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 53:4

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּבֵי רַבִּי שֵׁילָא אָמְרִי: שִׁילֹה שְׁמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question 'מה שמו' from step 23 with five opinions.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Five names, each based on a פסוק: שילה, ינון, חנינה, מנחם בן חזקיה, and חיוורא דבי רבי.

steps.title: רב נחמן: if משיח is alive now, he is like me
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן says that if משיח is among the living, he would be someone like himself, based on the פסוק that the ruler will come from among the people.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: If he is among the living, he is someone like me, as it says: 'Their mighty one will be from among them, and their ruler will come out from their midst.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן describes what kind of person משיח would be if he were alive in that generation, and he points to himself as an example.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says the leader will come 'from among them', meaning from a leader the people already have. רב נחמן uses this to say משיח would be someone who already leads the Jewish people, like himself.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said:

phrases.aramaic: אִי מִן חַיַּיָּא הוּא, כְּגוֹן אֲנָא,
phrases.english: If he is from among the living, he is someone like me,
as it is said: "And their mighty one shall be from themselves,
and their ruler shall come out from their midst."
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 30:21

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: אִי מִן חַיַּיָּא הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the topic of משיח's identity, now asking who he would be if he were alive in that generation.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If משיח is alive in this generation, he is someone who already leads the people, like רב נחמן.

steps.title: רב: like רבינו הקדוש if alive, like דניאל if from the dead
steps.stepSummary: רב says that if משיח is among the living, he is someone like רבינו הקדוש. If he is among the dead, he is someone like דניאל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: If he is among the living, he is someone like רבינו הקדוש. If he is among the dead, he is someone like דניאל, the beloved man.
steps.whatsHappening: רב gives his own version of who משיח would be. He covers two cases: someone alive now, or someone from the dead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן pointed to a leader with power. רב instead points to people known for great holiness: רבי יהודה הנשיא, and דניאל, whom the פסוק calls 'the beloved man'. רב also adds the possibility that משיח could be someone who already died.

keyTerms.meaning: Our holy teacher, רבי יהודה הנשיא
The beloved (precious) man, a title for דניאל

phrases.english: Rav said:
If he is from among the living,
he is someone like our holy Rebbi.
phrases.notes: This is רבי יהודה הנשיא, who wrote down the משנה.

phrases.english: If he is from among the dead,
he is someone like Daniel, the beloved man.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: אִי מִן חַיַּיָּא הוּא, כְּגוֹן רַבֵּינוּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A different view from רב נחמן's in step 25 about who משיח would be.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If משיח is alive, he is like רבינו הקדוש. If he is from the dead, he is like דניאל.

steps.title: הקב״ה will set up 'another דוד'
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה in the name of רב says that הקב״ה will set up another דוד, because the פסוק says 'אקים' (I will set up) in the future tense, not 'הקים' (He set up).
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: הקב״ה will in the future set up for them another דוד, as it says: 'They will serve ה׳ their God and דוד their king, whom I will set up for them.' It does not say 'הקים' (set up, in the past), but 'אקים' (I will set up).
steps.whatsHappening: רב teaches that משיח will be a new דוד. He proves it from the future-tense wording of a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק talks about 'דוד their king' in the time of the redemption. Since it uses the future tense 'אקים', it cannot mean the דוד who already lived and ruled. It must mean a new king called דוד.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav:
The Holy One, Blessed be He, will in the future
set up for them another David,
as it is said: "And they shall serve the Lord their God

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵת דָּוִד מַלְכָּם אֲשֶׁר אָקִים לָהֶם״.
phrases.english: and David their king, whom I will set up for them."
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 30:9

phrases.english: It does not say "set up" (in the past), but "I will set up."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: עָתִיד הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְהַעֲמִיד לָהֶם דָּוִד אַחֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another statement of רב about משיח: he will be a new דוד.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: משיח will be a new דוד, proven from the future-tense word 'אקים'.

steps.title: רב פפא: a פסוק says דוד himself will rule forever
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא asks אביי: But a פסוק says 'And דוד My servant will be their prince forever', which sounds like the original דוד.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said to אביי: But it is written: 'And דוד My servant will be their prince forever'?
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא challenges רב's idea of 'another דוד' using a פסוק in יחזקאל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק calls him 'דוד My servant', which sounds like the original דוד, and it says he will rule 'forever'. So it seems the original דוד himself will be the king, and not a new דוד.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said to Abaye:
But isn't it written:
"And David My servant shall be their prince forever"?
phrases.notes: יחזקאל 37:25

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב פָּפָּא לְאַבָּיֵי: וְהָכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's statement in step 27.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's teaching that הקב״ה will set up 'another דוד'.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: יחזקאל calls the future ruler 'דוד My servant', which suggests the original דוד will rule, not a new one.

steps.title: Like an emperor and his deputy
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that both will rule, like an emperor and a deputy emperor.
steps.simpleTranslation: Like an emperor and a half-emperor (deputy).
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers that both פסוקים are true: a new דוד will be king, and the original דוד will rule beside him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There will be two rulers at the same time. The new דוד, who is משיח, is the main king, like an emperor. The original דוד is the 'prince' (נשיא) next to him, like a deputy emperor. This fits both 'אקים' and 'דוד My servant'.
steps.whatToRemember: משיח will be a 'new דוד' (from 'אקים'), and the original דוד will also rule beside him as his second-in-command, like an emperor and his deputy.

phrases.english: Like an emperor and a half-emperor.
phrases.notes: This is אביי's answer. The new דוד is the main king, and the original דוד is his deputy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב פפא's challenge in step 28.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Harmonization: both פסוקים are true because two rulers share power.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק in יחזקאל seemed to mean that only the original דוד would rule, which would leave no room for a new דוד.
steps.terutzMaskana: A new דוד will be the emperor, and the original דוד will be the deputy (נשיא) beside him.

steps.title: Why does the פסוק warn those who long for the day of ה׳?
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמלאי opens a new teaching by asking what the פסוק in עמוס means when it says 'Woe to those who desire the day of ה׳… it is darkness and not light.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמלאי taught: What is the meaning of the פסוק, 'Woe to you who desire the day of ה׳. Why would you want this day of ה׳? It is darkness, and not light'?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמלאי quotes a puzzling פסוק and asks what it means. This sets up the parable that comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Wanting the day of ה׳, the great day of redemption, sounds like a good thing. So it is strange that the נביא says 'woe' to people who want it, and calls that day darkness. רבי שמלאי raises this puzzle so that he can solve it with a parable.

keyTerms.meaning: taught or expounded (explained a פסוק publicly)
What is the meaning of what is written? (a standard opening for explaining a פסוק)
the day of ה׳, the great future day of judgment and redemption
those who long for or desire

phrases.english: Rabbi Simlai taught:
What is the meaning of that which is written:
"Woe to you who desire the day of the Lord;
phrases.notes: עמוס 5:18

phrases.english: why would you have this day of the Lord?
It is darkness, and not light"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the discussion of who משיח will be to a new teaching about the day of redemption itself.

steps.title: The parable of the rooster and the bat
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמלאי explains the פסוק with a parable. A rooster and a bat both wait for light, and the rooster asks the bat why it wants light, since light belongs to the rooster.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is like a rooster and a bat who were both waiting for the light. The rooster said to the bat: 'I wait for the light because the light is mine. But you, why do you need light?'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמלאי answers his own question with a parable about a rooster and a bat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Daylight is good for the rooster, whose time to be active is the day. For the bat, daylight is no good at all. In the same way, the day of ה׳ is a blessing only for those it belongs to. For others it brings 'darkness and not light', so there is no reason for them to long for it.
steps.whatToRemember: The day of ה׳ is 'light' only for those it truly belongs to, just as daylight belongs to the rooster. Someone it does not belong to has no reason to long for it, like the bat.
